title: AI Agents Can Shop Now. Why Are Stores Shutting the Door? 3 Doors After Amazon Blocked Muse
description:
AI agents can shop for you, but whether the door opens is the store's call. There are three kinds of door: Amazon blocks everything, Target depends, Walmart opens the front door with rules. One comparison, the security guard at a shop door, makes it clear, along with three questions to ask before you hand over your wallet.
For anyone already using ChatGPT, Gemini or Meta AI who wants to know whether "AI, buy this for me" actually works yet, and for small business owners wondering whether to let AI agents onto their own sites.

You'll be able to tell apart:
・Door one, "it depends": a reporter at The Verge sent Meta's Muse to Target for face cream; a bot check stopped it, it got in the next day, then it was blocked again when she asked about mattresses. Target says it may depend on how that task was carried out and what safeguards the site has; the bot check stops every automated program, not just Muse
・Door two, "block everything": the pop-up Amazon showed Muse users one Sunday in September, its three reasons (Meta gave no advance notice, Muse doesn't identify itself as an agent, it appeared to capture login details), and Amazon's demand that Meta remove Amazon from Muse; Amazon's own agent on its platform; Amazon suing Perplexity last November, and a judge siding with Perplexity this August
・What happens when the door is open: The RealReal holds items in your cart for 20 minutes; the reporter had Muse put the 10 newest listings in at once, put them in again when time ran out, and keep it up all day; the responses from the CTO and a Meta spokesperson
・Door three, "front door with rules": Walmart's Agent Profiles, announced October 21 (a profile is created the first time an agent passes through the gateway, you link it to your own account, by default you approve every purchase or let it buy automatically within a $50/$100/$200 limit, and you can delete it any time), the terms for agents (no payment cards, nothing beyond your intent, only the data that's needed and allowed, returns as usual, blocked for violations), and agents see the same prices as people
・Three things to ask before handing an agent the job: will it ask me before buying, can I set a limit, which stores can't it get into; applied to the reporter's hunt for the lowest granola bar price

Every attempt by the reporter in this video was made by the reporter herself, as told in The Verge's report of October 22, 2026; Amazon's pop-up blocking Muse and its three reasons (citing GeekWire), and The Verge buying tank tops on Amazon with Muse before the block, come from The Verge's report of September 21, 2026; Walmart's Agent Profiles, Agent Gateway and agent terms come from Walmart's press release of October 21, 2026. This channel did not test any of the agents itself; the lines starting "My view" and "Personally" are my own opinions. I found no news on whether Amazon still blocks Muse after the report date; Walmart says Agent Profiles are "launching in the next month", and Agent Gateway will open first as a beta for businesses and developers, so go by Walmart's announcements for the actual timing. This video is not purchase, investment or legal advice.

What's the one thing you'd most like an AI agent to buy for you? Tell me in the comments.

chapters.open: Can AI agents shop for me?
chapters.realreal: What if the door is open?

6czz.text: On October 21, Walmart opened its door to AI agents; a month earlier, Amazon shut its door.

qcpx.text: The next day, a reporter at The Verge wrote up how she sent Meta's agent, Muse, out to shop.

rwk8.text: You might think: can't AI agents already shop for me?

h54m.text: They can. An agent will search for products, compare prices, fill your cart and place the order.

fpjh.text: But whether the door opens is the store's call.

2t6w.text: If its price check is missing a store, it may not tell you.

t3xu.text: After this, you'll tell three kinds of door apart, ask three questions before handing over your wallet, and know how Walmart's limit works.

g8uj.text: Can it really buy things? The reporter first sent it to Target for a jar of face cream, and a bot check stopped it at the door.

5e27.text: The next day, the same instruction got it in.

ztxw.text: A few minutes later she asked about mattresses, and it was shut out again.

vht2.text: This is the first kind of door: it depends.

wx69.text: Like a guard at the door watching how you walk in: Target said it may depend on how that task was done and the site's safeguards.

ve6e.text: The comparison stops here: a guard stops people, while a bot check stops every automated program, and Muse is just one of them.

taip.text: Next she gave it the simplest job: find the lowest price per granola bar.

jwwd.text: It found three stores: Sam's Club, Walmart and Costco. Which one is missing?

p4ma.text: Then it added a note of its own: Amazon might be cheaper,

9skt.text: but it was hard-blocked, so it couldn't confirm.

vijc.text: When you compare prices today, you open three tabs; a missing store jumps out at a glance.

qbyv.text: With an agent, you only learn of the missing store if it's willing to say so.

fidw.text: And one West Coast grocery store doesn't even deliver to New York.

5pwn.text: Waiting for replies, checking more stores, sorting out delivery: the reporter reckoned doing it herself was probably faster.

sx6e.text: My view: the biggest problem isn't whether it buys the wrong thing, but that the stores it can see are incomplete.

n3fs.text: The reporter says what it may really be good for is tasks where you already know what to buy and just need the lowest price.

wcyk.text: So why did Amazon shut its door?

erea.text: The shut door from the opening: one Sunday, Muse users opened Amazon and found a notice.

6vzr.text: "Continued unauthorized AI agent access violates Amazon's Conditions of Use,

8swe.text: to which our customers have agreed."

a7bt.text: The second kind of door: block everything. A notice at the door; however you walk, you're not getting in.

ip66.text: You might wonder: does Amazon block it because it might buy things at random?

avjj.text: No. There are three reasons: Meta didn't notify Amazon in advance;

fsmh.text: Muse doesn't identify itself as an agent when it browses sites;

k2gc.text: and it appeared to capture customers' login details.

fwer.text: An Amazon spokesperson said apps that shop other stores for customers should operate openly,

359n.text: and respect service provider decisions about whether or not to participate.

vf3r.text: But Amazon has an agent on its own platform: it watches prices, reorders automatically and buys by rules you set.

dxbj.text: Muse isn't the first: last November, Amazon sued Perplexity, whose agent also shopped on the site.

vaf7.text: This year, a judge sided with Perplexity; Amazon also removed product names and images from its confirmation emails.

xiq6.text: My view: Amazon's reasons hold up; but it builds agents too, so this is a business fight, not just security.

druk.text: Is Amazon still blocking Muse? I found no news since the report, so I'll assume it still is.

ny56.text: And a store whose door is unlocked and really open?

ysce.text: The reporter went to a store with an open door: the luxury resale site The RealReal.

yieg.text: This store's rule: an item in your cart is held for you for 20 minutes, and no one else can take it.

emy8.text: The reporter had Muse put a brand's 10 newest clothing listings into the cart, all at once.

xgqr.text: She had no intention of buying.

278c.text: When time ran out, she had it add them again; and so on, all day.

desu.text: The hand that hits refresh when you chase a limited drop: it did that for her all day.

y2ie.text: Shoppers outside effectively couldn't get a single item; in the end, the reporter stopped it herself.

y46v.text: She said that if she were less honest, the holds these rules allow could run forever.

g8eg.text: What worries the reporter is that soon she'll have to compete with other people's agents too.

62fp.text: You might wonder: so why don't stores block it?

mdbm.text: The RealReal's CTO said it's open to third-party agents, letting them browse, log in and interact,

v2ap.text: with safeguards against automated activity that could disrupt the customer experience.

8eug.text: Meta's spokesperson said users can take over at any time, and Muse is designed to always ask permission before buying;

a35m.text: for things a human couldn't do, like buying out an event's tickets, it applies ethical browsing principles.

fp4t.text: Buying out a whole show is beyond even the fast fingers you trained grabbing concert tickets.

cqnx.text: So has any store spelled out the rules and let agents in through the front door?

x8e3.text: Yes. Walmart's press release: agents can shop for customers, but by its rules.

mki8.text: The third kind of door: a front door with rules.

8fej.text: The store opens a separate door with numbered tickets: register first; by default every purchase needs your nod, as the boss, and you can set a limit.

2y4r.text: This front door is called Agent Gateway; it uses MCP so agents talk to the system directly, with no clicking page by page.

c72f.text: Registering means a profile: when an AI agent first passes the gateway, Walmart creates one automatically.

evku.text: You sign in to your own Walmart account to link it, and only Walmart sees this step;

hdi7.text: The nod means approval: by default, every purchase needs your nod.

8rxu.text: That's the limit: you set an amount, and under it the agent buys on its own; the press release's examples are $50, $100 and $200.

zmdp.text: Here's the catch: a limit doesn't mean you won't be asked; under it, Walmart may still ask you to approve again.

wv4s.text: You might wonder: can it get my credit card, then?

35d6.text: No. The terms say it can't get payment card data, or add or change your payment methods;

u8h7.text: it can't go beyond what you intend, and only gets the data this trip needs and you allow;

mtuc.text: Wrong item? Returns work as usual, even if the agent didn't act as expected; break the rules, and Walmart blocks it.

aezm.text: That ticket isn't real; it's the agent profile in your account. And agents see the same prices as people.

fezk.text: My view: spelling out the rules first, with your own approval for every purchase by default, beats blocking outright or a free-for-all.

sdnk.text: So, should I use it myself?

pgy9.text: To decide, test it on the reporter's lowest-price hunt: does it ask before buying? Meta says it does.

qkgp.text: Can you set a limit? Meta's response gives no answer.

ecah.text: Which store bars it? Amazon. This time it said so itself.

5i3t.text: Personally, I'd only use it when I know what to buy and just need the price check and order, and have it ask me before every purchase.

dkkh.text: Do three things now. First, before handing over a task, ask it: which stores can't you get into?

ippg.text: Second, have it ask you before every purchase.

q3kh.text: Third, where a store offers a limit, like Walmart's upcoming profiles, set it before sending the agent out.

za58.text: Whether the door opens is the store's call: Amazon's is shut, Target's depends, and Walmart's is open, with rules.

56u3.text: What's the one thing you'd most like an AI agent to buy for you? Tell me in the comments.

e338.text: If you want every video to leave you with a judgment you can act on, subscribe.

**out**
thumbnail.sub: Amazon: no. Target: maybe. Walmart: yes
